overview.summary: Patent attorneys, called patent agents in some countries, help inventors and companies protect inventions through patents, combining technical and legal knowledge.
overview.problems: They help people secure exclusive rights to new inventions and avoid infringing other people's rights.
overview.worksWith: Inventors, engineers and scientists, companies, patent offices and other lawyers.
overview.workplaces: Patent law firms, companies' legal departments and patent offices, mostly in offices.

timeline.title: Review the invention
timeline.description: The attorney reads the inventor's description and drawings.
timeline.why: You need to understand an invention before you can protect it.

timeline.title: Searching existing patents
timeline.description: The attorney searches public databases to see whether similar ideas already exist.
timeline.why: An invention must be new to be patented.

timeline.title: Drafting the application
timeline.description: The attorney writes a precise description and the claims that define what is protected.
timeline.why: The wording decides how strong the protection is.

timeline.title: Talking to inventors
timeline.description: The attorney asks questions and explains the process and costs.
timeline.why: Inventors need to understand their choices.

timeline.title: Responding to patent offices
timeline.description: The attorney answers objections from examiners and amends applications.
timeline.why: Most applications need some discussion before they are granted.

timeline.title: Deadlines
timeline.description: Patent processes have strict time limits in each country.
timeline.why: A missed date can lose valuable rights.

challenges: Qualifying usually needs both a science or engineering degree and further legal training and exams.
Drafting is slow and demands extreme precision.
Deadlines are strict, and a missed date can lose rights.
Billing and time pressure affect work in firms.
There are fewer roles than in many careers, so competition can be strong.
workEnvironment: Mostly offices, with reading, writing and meetings with inventors and patent offices. Hours are usually regular but can be long near deadlines. Some work remotely or across countries.
rewards: Working at the edge of new technology
A mix of science and law
tradeoffs: Pay and routes that vary by country

activity.title: Describe a pretend invention and search for similar ones
steps: Imagine a simple invention, such as a lunch box that keeps food cold without ice.
Write a one-page description, then three sentences saying what is new about it.
Using a free public patent search site, such as a national patent office's, look for similar ideas.
Note how yours differs from what you find.
Note whether careful, precise writing felt interesting.
activity.outcome: You practise explaining an idea precisely and checking whether it is new.
activity.safety: This is a learning exercise only and not legal advice. Do not share a real invention idea publicly or online before asking an adult, because doing so can affect the chance of patenting it.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
